parts.title: Learning to ride
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
I learnt to ride a bike when I was eight, but I was much slower than my friends. My cousin Max could ride without help when he was five, and he liked to remind me of this. It made me determined to improve.

My grandfather offered to teach me in the park on Sunday mornings. He was seventy at the time, and he could not run beside me, so he stood in the middle of the path and cheered. On my first try, I fell into a bush. On my second, I rode five metres before crashing into a bench.

The turning point came on the fourth Sunday. My grandfather told me to stop looking at my feet and look at the end of the path instead. I did what he said, and suddenly the bike seemed to balance itself. I rode right round the pond without stopping, and my grandfather clapped as if I had won a race.

Now I cycle to school every day. Last year, I even overtook Max on a hill. I have never mentioned it to him, but I think he knows.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer want to improve?
options: His school had a big race
His parents were disappointed in him
questions.explanation: Max liked to remind him he rode earlier.

questions.prompt: How did the grandfather help?
options: He encouraged from the middle of the path
He rode beside him on his own bike
He ran beside the bike all the way
He held the back of the seat
questions.explanation: He stood in the middle of the path and cheered.

questions.prompt: What was the secret of success?
options: Pedalling as fast as he possibly could
Using a smaller bicycle than before
Wearing a helmet all the time
Looking at the end of the path
questions.explanation: He stopped looking at his feet and looked at the end of the path.

questions.prompt: How did the grandfather react to the success?
options: He told him to try again
He took a photograph of him
He gave him a brand new bike
questions.explanation: He clapped as if the boy had won a race.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about Max now?
options: He once overtook Max on a hill
questions.explanation: Last year he overtook Max on a hill.

parts.title: A cycle to work scheme
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
More and more people in our city are cycling to work, and the council wants to encourage even more. [1] Last year, it spent two million pounds on new cycle lanes that are separated from the traffic, so that cyclists feel much safer than before.

The council has also started a new scheme with local companies. [2] In return, the companies must provide showers and safe places for bikes.

Workers say that the changes are making a difference. [3] One office worker, Anita, says she now saves twenty pounds a week on bus tickets and arrives at work feeling fresher. [4] Not everyone is convinced, though. Some drivers complain that the cycle lanes take space from the roads.

[5] The council promises to keep listening to everybody and says that more changes will follow next year.
sentences: Cycling is also cheaper than going by car or by bus.
This debate is likely to continue for some time.
The number of cyclists has gone up by a third in two years.
Employees who cycle to work get a small payment for every journey.
More than half of them are under thirty.
It has already made a number of changes to the streets.
The company was started more than fifty years ago.
The company started its own bike shop last spring.

gaps.explanation: The council has already made changes, and the next sentence gives an example.
The scheme gives a payment to employees, and "in return" the companies provide showers.
Cycling numbers rising is what workers say, followed by a personal example.
"Also cheaper" adds to the benefits, before the objection from some drivers.
The debate will continue is a fitting link to the council promising to listen.

parts.title: Bike safety tips
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Cycling is a great way to travel, but it is important to stay safe on the road, especially in the city. First of all, always wear a helmet, even [1] your journey is short. Make sure your lights work [2] it gets dark, and wear bright clothes so that drivers can see you. Never use your phone [3] you are riding. Always give a clear signal with your hand before you turn. Remember that red traffic lights are for cyclists [4] well as for cars. You should also check your brakes and tyres once [5] week. If you follow these simple rules, [6] will enjoy many safe and happy journeys.

gaps.explanation: Lights should work "when" it gets dark.
Never use your phone "while" you are riding.
We say "once a week", so the article "a" is needed here.

parts.title: A talk about the cycling club
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: peter
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Cycling Club. I’m Peter, the club secretary, and I’ll tell you how a Sunday works. Let’s start with the time. The fast group leaves at eight, but those riders have been cycling for years. The group for new riders meets at nine, so you’ll have a calm start, with a coffee. Where do we meet? Years ago it was outside the station, but the car park there is too small and the taxis get angry, so we moved. Now we gather outside the library, next to the fountain. Please don’t go to the station, because nobody will be there. Now the distance. Each Sunday, the easiest ride is twenty kilometres, on flat roads by the river. The medium group does forty, with some hills, and when you’re stronger you can move up. But please don’t try forty on your first day. Safety is important. We lend you a bright jacket in the first month, and gloves are nice in winter, but you don’t have to wear them. The one thing that everyone must have, with no exceptions, is a helmet. If you don’t have one, we can’t let you ride. Next, money. Membership is thirty pounds a year. Students pay half, fifteen, if they show a card. That includes insurance and the club newsletter. After the ride we always stop for tea and cake. You pay for your own cake, but it’s the best part of the day. Finally, our summer trip. Last year we went to the mountains and it was very hard work, so this year we’ve chosen something easier. In July we’ll cycle to the coast, and sleep in a hostel near the beach. I hope many of you will join us. Thanks for listening.

gaps.explanation: The fast group leaves at eight, but the group for new riders meets at nine.

gaps.prompt: The meeting point is outside the ___
gaps.explanation: They used to meet outside the station, but now they gather outside the library.
The easiest ride is twenty kilometres; the medium group does forty.

gaps.prompt: The only compulsory item of equipment is a ___
gaps.explanation: The jacket is lent and gloves are optional, but everyone must have a helmet.

gaps.prompt: A year of membership costs adults ___ pounds
gaps.explanation: Membership is thirty pounds a year; students pay half, fifteen.

gaps.prompt: The summer trip in July goes to the ___
gaps.explanation: Last year’s trip was to the mountains; in July they will cycle to the coast.

parts.title: A cyclist
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Marisol, you cycled across Europe. Why did you decide to do it?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Everybody thinks it’s about sport, but I’m not a racer, and I don’t need a trip to keep fit. I’d travelled by plane and train all my life, and I realised that I never really saw anything. From a train window, villages pass in seconds. On a bike, you see the baker open his door and you hear the church bells. I wanted to go slowly enough to notice things.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: How far did you travel?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: My first plan was four hundred kilometres, just through France. Then I added Italy, and then I kept going. Friends guessed fourteen thousand, because they thought I was crazy, but my counter said just over four thousand, in ninety days. That is quite enough for me.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Where did you sleep?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Mostly in a tent. One night on a beach in Spain was lovely, and in Switzerland I stayed in a hotel, a very expensive one, because of a storm. But my favourite was a farmer in Slovenia who let me sleep in his barn, with the cows next to me. The hay was warm, and in the morning his wife gave me bread and honey.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Did anything go wrong?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: The police never stopped me, although I was nervous about border checks, and I didn’t lose anything important, only a small bag with socks. But in Austria my chain broke on a mountain road, and I didn’t have the right tool. A man in a van stopped, and he mended it in ten minutes with his own tools. He refused to take any money.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: What was your best moment?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Arriving in the capital cities was exciting, but they were crowded, so it wasn’t the best. Crossing the border into Spain was nice, and I cried a little. But the best moment was on a mountain pass in Italy, when after four hours of climbing I could see the whole valley, and I shouted with joy. Nobody heard me, which was perfect.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Will you go again?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Yes. People ask me to write a book, but I’m not interested, and my friends want me to go with them, but I need to go alone. Next year I want to do another trip, because what I loved most was the freedom. I woke up every day with no timetable and no plan, and I miss it already. I even keep my tent on top of the wardrobe, ready, in case I get a free week.

questions.prompt: Why did Marisol want to cycle across Europe?
options: To train for a big race
To notice things around her slowly
questions.explanation: She says it is not about sport or keeping fit; from trains she saw nothing, so she wanted to go slowly enough to notice things.

questions.prompt: How far did she travel?
questions.explanation: Four hundred was her first plan and fourteen thousand was her friends’ guess; her counter said just over four thousand.

questions.prompt: Where did she sleep once?

questions.explanation: The police never stopped her and she lost nothing important; a man in a van mended her broken chain.

questions.explanation: She is not interested in a book and she needs to go alone; she loved the freedom and misses it already.
